per_question.question: According to the SVM notes, what is the core idea of Support Vector Machines regarding the selection of the hyperplane?
per_question.reference_answer: SVM tries to maximize the gap (margin) between points and the line so that the highest margin hyperplane performs best on unseen data.

basic.answer: The core idea of Support Vector Machines is to select a hyperplane that classifies data points as widely as possible by maximizing the gap between the points and the line [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.1]. This approach aims to increase the margin so that the model performs better on unseen data compared to other lines [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.1].

By choosing the hyperplane that classifies points as widely as possible, the model aims to improve its performance on unseen data in the future [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.1]. This approach is summarized as trying to maximize the distance between the points and the line [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.1].

per_question.question: How does the SVM notes describe the relationship between the hyperparameter C and the regularization parameter lambda?

basic.answer: The notes describe the relationship between the hyperparameter C and the regularization parameter lambda as being inversely proportional, expressed as C ∝ 1/λ [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.5]. This connection is drawn by comparing the SVM loss function, which includes a regularization term and a hinge loss, to the logistic regression loss function that uses lambda for L2 regularization [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.5].

agentic.answer:
The SVM notes describe the relationship between the hyperparameter C and the regularization parameter lambda as an inverse proportionality, specifically stating that C is proportional to 1/lambda [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.5].

To understand how this works in practice, the notes compare the SVM loss function to logistic regression, where lambda is the hyperparameter controlling L2 regularization [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.5]. In the SVM formulation, the loss is the sum of a regularization term (||w||/2) and a hinge loss term weighted by C [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.5].

The notes explain the practical implications of this relationship through the value of C:
1. If C is very high, classification error gets more weightage than margin error, which means the model focuses on reducing misclassification even if it has to reduce the margin [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.5].
2. If C is very small, the model ignores classification error and focuses more on maximizing the margin [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.5].

This trade-off is part of the soft margin SVM formulation, which allows for some classification errors to handle data that is not perfectly linearly separable [SVM_Notes.pdf, p.4].
